_comment: Template sections are the backbone of three separate mechanisms: (1) the generated artifact's structure, (2) the G4 scorecard rows -- one row per section with scorable:true, and (3) the fixture transport's content plan. A section's `fixtureBullets` are the raw material each writer voice selects from, which is how three writers produce genuinely different drafts of the same template.

sections.heading: Problem Statement
fixtureBullets: Delivery artifacts are produced by hand or by ad-hoc prompting, so quality varies by author rather than by difficulty.
Traceability from business outcome to verifying test is weak enough that nobody can answer "is this requirement tested?" without a manual trawl.
Review cycles are the bottleneck, not authoring: a document waits days for a reviewer who then skims it.
The pilot measured ~70% artifact accuracy, which is useful only if a human knows *which* 30% is wrong.
Teams that adopted ad-hoc AI assistance got faster first drafts and slower approvals.

sections.heading: Target Outcomes
fixtureBullets: Cut preparation effort for lifecycle artifacts by ~20% against the pilot baseline, measured at G4 rather than asserted.
Make every published artifact carry provenance sufficient to reconstruct how it was produced.
Reduce time-to-first-reviewable-draft from days to under an hour for design documents.
Give reviewers a defensible place to spend attention instead of reading three drafts end to end.
Establish an accuracy baseline per skill so later prompt changes can be judged rather than argued about.

sections.heading: Users and Personas
fixtureBullets: Product Manager: owns vetting documents and discovery ideas; owns gates G3, G4 and G5.
Architect: owns high- and low-level design; needs the design review to be evidence-based.
Developer: owns story implementation and pull-request proposals; owns G2 and G5 for code.
Platform Engineer: owns configuration, the model registry, budgets and knowledge bases.
Security and Compliance: consumes the audit trail; never needs to trust a narrative.

sections.heading: Scope
fixtureBullets: In scope: one governed thread from idea to tested pull-request proposal across three agent families.
In scope: three ways to start a run -- by agent, by action, by lifecycle stage.
Out of scope permanently: autonomous commit, push, merge, deploy, pipeline trigger or change submission.
Out of scope for this release: shared hosting, SSO, role-based access beyond a single workstation user.
Deferred: governed memory, review lenses, and skills export/import.

sections.heading: Functional Requirements
fixtureBullets: A run shall be startable only through a declared input schema, so every input is validatable, costable and recordable.
Three writers on three distinct model families shall draft independently and review every draft including their own.
A Captain shall adjudicate and produce a verdict in which every suggestion is attributed to its source candidate.
A human shall choose one base candidate and any subset of suggestions, as a single decision.
No write to an external system shall occur without a current, explicit, single-use approval bound to that exact version.
Section-by-section human accuracy scoring shall be mandatory before a document artifact is published.

sections.heading: Non-Functional Requirements
fixtureBullets: Cost: a pre-run estimate in premium requests, with per-run and per-user-daily budgets enforced server-side.
Reliability: a server restart shall lose no completed writer output.
Security: no secrets, personal data or restricted data in prompts, logs, artifacts or telemetry.
Accessibility: WCAG 2.2 AA in both themes and keyboard-only completion of the whole thread.
Auditability: the event stream is append-only and sufficient to reconstruct the run.

sections.heading: Risks and Mitigations
fixtureBullets: Reviewers rubber-stamp AI output. Mitigated by contested-candidate marking and mandatory section scoring.
Council cost grows with writer count. Mitigated by budgets, plan-first mode and a visible pre-run estimate.
Dependence on a single model provider. Mitigated by a provider abstraction with no vendor binding in code.
Target repositories are not AI-ready, so output is generic. Mitigated by a readiness assessment before use.
Knowledge bases may be unlicensed, which removes most of the measured accuracy.

sections.heading: Success Metrics
fixtureBullets: Mean section accuracy per skill, from G4 scorecards rather than from self-report.
Effort saved percentage per artifact, captured at G4 against a manual-effort estimate.
Premium requests per published artifact, trended by skill and model family.
Proportion of runs published without a quality-threshold override.
Count of writes performed without an approval: must remain exactly zero.

sections.heading: Open Questions
fixtureBullets: Which model families are enabled by policy for this team?
Who is the named decision authority for this document?
Which Confluence space and parent page receive published artifacts?

sections.heading: Epic Summary
fixtureBullets: The epic establishes a governed path from a requirement to a reviewed code change.
Scope is bounded by the approved high-level design and the non-functional envelope agreed at Solution Lock.
Delivery is sequenced so each story is independently demonstrable.

sections.heading: Stories
fixtureBullets: As a reviewer, I want contested drafts marked, so that I spend my attention where the writers disagreed.
As a product manager, I want a pre-run cost estimate, so that I can decide whether a council run is worth it.
As an approver, I want the approval bound to the exact version I reviewed, so that a later edit cannot ride along.
As a developer, I want to choose between plans before any code runs, so that execution happens once against the right plan.
As a platform engineer, I want budgets enforced server-side, so that a client bug cannot drain the daily allowance.
As an auditor, I want an append-only event log, so that I can reconstruct a run without trusting a summary.
As a quality engineer, I want test counters to read "not measured" when unparsed, so that a counter never contradicts the diff.

sections.heading: Acceptance Criteria
fixtureBullets: Given three writers on three distinct families, when a run completes, then exactly nine reviews exist and self-reviews are excluded from the peer average.
Given a candidate with an unresolved placeholder, when publication is attempted, then it is blocked and the placeholder is named.
Given an approval that has been consumed, when publication is retried, then it is rejected as already used.
Given a target that changed after the proposal was built, when approval is attempted, then it is rejected as stale.
Given an incomplete scorecard, when approval is attempted, then it is blocked until every section is scored.

sections.heading: Dependencies
fixtureBullets: Approved high-level design for the epic.
Model families enabled by policy for the council.
Write access to the target systems of record under the operator's own identity.

sections.heading: Context and Drivers
fixtureBullets: The change introduces an assurance step into an existing intent-registration flow without altering its public contract.
Primary driver is auditability: every decision must be reconstructable after the fact.
A secondary driver is cost control, because the expensive operation is invoked per request.
Constraint: the solution runs on a single workstation with no inbound network exposure.
Constraint: no credential may reach the component that executes untrusted content.

sections.heading: Component Design
fixtureBullets: An API layer owns validation, the error envelope and idempotency; it holds no orchestration logic.
A single orchestration engine drives declared phases; per-artifact behaviour is configuration, not code.
A provider abstraction resolves logical model names to concrete models and meters every call.
A policy component owns path resolution, redaction, budget checks and secret scanning -- each in exactly one place.
A proposal-and-approval component is the only path to an external write.
Integration adapters are mutually isolated and may not import the engine.

sections.heading: Data Design
fixtureBullets: An append-only event log is the source of truth; every projection is derived from it.
Runtime entities are immutable once approved, so provenance stays resolvable.
Content is stored content-addressed, separately from metadata, to keep the relational store small.
A monotonic sequence per session supports resume-by-sequence on the event stream.
The cost ledger is a first-class table, not a derived report, so every usage view reconciles to one total.

sections.heading: Integration Design
fixtureBullets: Every adapter implements one publish contract and ships a dry-run mode returning the exact intended change.
A deterministic per-target idempotency key is derived at proposal time and reused across every attempt.
An ambiguous failure -- a timeout after send -- is treated as possibly applied: probe first, never blind-retry.
Partial failure is reported per item, and only failed items may be retried.
The source-control adapter proposes pull requests and has no push capability at all.

sections.heading: Security Design
fixtureBullets: Trust boundaries are enumerated, and each has one named control rather than a general assurance.
Model output, repository content and retrieved knowledge are untrusted data in a delimited channel, never instructions.
Code execution runs credential-free with allow-listed egress and is destroyed after the run.
Generated code is scanned for credential-like strings, and a positive finding blocks the proposal.
Deployment and change execution are unreachable by an agent in any release, with or without approval.

sections.heading: NFR Considerations
fixtureBullets: Latency: the comparison view must stay interactive with three eight-thousand-word documents.
Cost: per-run and per-user-daily budgets are mandatory configuration; startup fails if unset.
Reliability: writers execute concurrently and one failure degrades the run rather than aborting it.
Recoverability: daily local backup plus export; no availability objective is claimed for a local tool.
Observability: per-run models, premium requests and durations per writer are recorded for every run.

sections.heading: Alternatives Considered
fixtureBullets: A per-agent orchestrator was rejected: five agent families would become five code paths that drift.
A single-model generator was rejected: correlated errors defeat the review mechanism entirely.
Direct provider APIs were rejected in favour of an abstraction, to avoid a vendor binding in application code.
A hosted multi-user deployment was deferred, keeping the seams open rather than building the planes.
An in-process sandbox was rejected for production use, retained only where no container runtime exists.

sections.heading: Risks and Open Items
fixtureBullets: Container runtime availability on managed workstations is unconfirmed.
The approved model catalogue is not yet fixed, which blocks the registry's concrete entries.
Required custom fields on the target issue tracker are unknown and will surface as publish rejections.

sections.heading: Scope and Inputs
fixtureBullets: This design elaborates the approved high-level design to implementation detail for one epic.
It assumes the component boundaries of the high-level design and does not revisit them.
Anything not named here is explicitly out of this design's scope.

sections.heading: Module Decomposition
fixtureBullets: Each module declares its permitted imports, and the rule is enforced in continuous integration rather than by convention.
Path resolution exists in exactly one module; a second resolver is a traversal defect waiting to happen.
Model-name-to-display-name mapping exists in exactly one module, because the pilot showed one model three ways in one flow.
The run status string is produced in exactly one place, because the pilot showed a spinner beside a finished result.
Phase handlers are uniform: each takes a run context and returns events, so the driver stays artifact-agnostic.

sections.heading: Interface Contracts
fixtureBullets: Every endpoint validates its body against a schema before any side effect, and rejects with field-level detail.
No endpoint accepts a policy decision from the client: budget, path, approval validity and model distinctness are server-side only.
Every state-changing endpoint is idempotent by nature or by key.
One error envelope shape is returned on every non-2xx response, carrying a stable problem code.
The event stream emits a monotonic sequence as its identifier, and replays from a supplied last-seen value.

sections.heading: Data Structures
fixtureBullets: Identifiers are opaque and type-prefixed; clients must not parse them.
Timestamps are UTC with milliseconds, in one format everywhere.
Amounts are integers in minor units with an explicit currency, never floating point.
Review records carry an explicit self-review flag rather than being inferred by comparing identifiers.
Candidate aggregates persist the evaluator score spread, because the contested threshold is read from it.

sections.heading: Key Algorithms
fixtureBullets: Quorum: at least two settled candidates are required to enter review; with one, skip to the human gate and mark degraded.
Peer average: self-reviews are excluded from the mean and displayed separately.
Contested detection: a candidate whose evaluator scores span more than twenty points is marked for attention.
Consensus extraction: a strength or concern raised by two or more evaluators is promoted to the consensus panel.
Cost estimation: writer count multiplied by resolved-model multipliers multiplied by expected calls per phase.

sections.heading: Error Handling
fixtureBullets: One writer failing with quorum intact continues the run and marks it degraded with a named cause.
A per-writer timeout fails only that writer; a run wall-clock timeout fails the run but preserves settled candidates.
A Captain failure preserves candidates and reviews, and offers retry, a cheaper mode, or proceeding with no verdict -- clearly labelled.
A sandbox failure yields no partial proposal and destroys the sandbox.
Degradation is never silent: every degraded run names its cause in the interface and in provenance.

sections.heading: Test Design
fixtureBullets: Every must-have requirement maps to a named test, and the test name carries the requirement identifier.
Integration tests run against recorded fixtures, so continuous integration is deterministic and free.
Live-model evaluations are scheduled, never on the pull-request path, because they are non-deterministic and cost money.
Negative tests are first-class: a blocked write is as important to prove as a successful one.
Boundary rules and non-negotiables are checked mechanically, not asserted in review.

sections.heading: Deployment and Configuration
fixtureBullets: Configuration is split per stage and merged at build time; the merged artifact is build output and never hand-edited.
The server refuses to start on invalid configuration; there is no degraded-mode startup.
Prompts are immutable versioned files, referenced by explicit version and never by "latest".

sections.heading: Understanding
fixtureBullets: The story adds an assurance check to the intent-registration path and must not change the existing response contract.
Two callers exist today; both must keep working without modification.
The change is additive: a new validator plus wiring, not a rewrite of the mapper.

sections.heading: Planned Steps
fixtureBullets: Add an assurance-level enumeration alongside the existing intent model rather than overloading an existing field.
Introduce a validator with a single public entry point so the call site stays one line.
Wire the validator into the registration service behind the existing feature boundary.
Extend the mapper to carry the assurance level through to the response object.
Add unit tests for each assurance level including the rejection path.
Add an integration test proving the existing callers are unaffected.

sections.heading: Files to Change
fixtureBullets: A new enumeration file for assurance levels.
A new validator class with its unit test.
The registration service, to call the validator.
The mapper, to propagate the resolved level.
The existing service test, extended rather than replaced.

sections.heading: Verification
fixtureBullets: Unit tests cover every enumeration value plus the null and unknown inputs.
An existing-behaviour test proves the public contract is unchanged.
A negative test proves an unknown assurance level is rejected rather than defaulted.

sections.heading: Risks and Rollback
fixtureBullets: Blast radius is one service and one mapper; no schema change and no migration.
Rollback is the revert of a single change set, with no data to undo.
The main risk is a silent default on an unknown level, which the negative test exists to prevent.

sections.heading: Summary
fixtureBullets: The change adds an assurance validator and propagates its result, across five files with no public contract change.
Structure follows the existing package layout, and the new class has a single responsibility.
Test coverage accompanies the change rather than following it.

sections.heading: Findings
fixtureBullets: [MEDIUM] The validator returns a boolean where the caller needs to distinguish "invalid" from "not applicable"; a result type would prevent a silent false.
[LOW] The new enumeration has no explicit unknown member, so a future value deserialises to null and takes the happy path.
[MEDIUM] The mapper change is untested for the null assurance case, which is reachable from the existing callers.
[LOW] A log line includes the full intent payload; it should be reduced to the identifier before merge.
[HIGH] The rejection path throws a generic runtime exception, which the existing handler maps to a 500 rather than a 422.

sections.heading: Test Assessment
fixtureBullets: Positive paths are covered for every enumeration value.
The null input case is not covered, and it is reachable.
No test asserts the status code produced by the rejection path.

sections.heading: Recommendation
fixtureBullets: Request changes: address the rejection-path status mapping and add the null-assurance test before merge.
The remaining findings are non-blocking and can follow in a separate change.
